facts.fact: Julio Cesar Garavello described it as a species new to science in 1990, from Suriname.
The original description appeared in the Bulletin Zoologisch Museum, volume 12, issue 11, pages 161–170.
The same paper gave new diagnoses of two related species, Leporinus granti and Leporinus gomesi, from the Aripuanã River basin in Mato Grosso, Brazil.
The type locality is about 27 km south of Village Dam on Sara Creek, Brokopondo District, Suriname. The holotype is ZMA 107562.
Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes now treats it as a valid species in the genus Hypomasticus, as Hypomasticus nijsseni.
AQUATAB lists it as Hypomasticus nijsseni, with Leporinus nijsseni as a synonym.
It belongs to the family Anostomidae, subfamily Leporininae.
The species name honours Dr Han Nijssen (1935–2013), a Dutch ichthyologist who specialised in Corydoras.
The genus name Leporinus comes from the Latin lepus, leporis, meaning hare or rabbit.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern (assessed 1 March 2007).
It has an elongated body, an arched back and a narrower tail.
Its body is yellowish gold with scattered black spots of different sizes.
Its dorsal, pectoral and caudal fins are transparent. Some individuals have orange-yellow pelvic fins, and the anal fin can match the body colour.
It reaches about 17 cm total length.
It is found in the Saramacca Creek and Suriname River basins in South America.
Eschmeyer's Catalog lists it from Brazil, French Guiana and Suriname.
The video says it is native to the Suriname and Saramacca river basins in French Guiana and Suriname.
It lives in fast-flowing, rocky waters.
During the rainy season it migrates into flooded forest. When the water falls, some fish are stranded inland in lakes and ponds.
It is a tropical, benthopelagic freshwater fish.
It is becoming popular in the hobby for its colouring and because it is less aggressive than other leporinus such as the banded leporinus.
It can reach up to 18 cm, so it needs a suitably large aquarium.
It nibbles delicate plant leaves when no algae are present, so it is not suited to a planted aquarium.
The tank needs a tight-fitting lid because the fish is an excellent jumper and can jump long distances.
An ideal setup has a sandy bottom, lumps of rock and pieces of driftwood.
It is described as remarkably hardy.
It sometimes swims head-down, grazing continually on algae.
In the aquarium it readily takes good-quality dried foods such as granules, flakes and sinking pellets.
Live, frozen or freeze-dried bloodworm, daphnia and tubifex once or twice a week are beneficial but not essential.
Give bloodworm only as an occasional treat, as it is hard to digest and can cause blockages.
It is highly active.
It is generally peaceful with fish of similar size, but adults may be somewhat territorial towards each other.
It can nip fins, so tank mates should be chosen carefully.
It can make an excellent community fish in a well-planned aquarium.
The sexes are hard to tell apart. The only noticeable difference is that adult females have rounder bellies than males.
In the wild, distinct pairs breed in densely weedy areas, according to FishBase.
